title: Chuck Yeager, 1947 — faster than sound, with two broken ribs
sources: Wikipedia: Chuck Yeager — first human to officially break the sound barrier, 14 October 1947, in the Bell X-1 at 45,000 ft; two nights before, he went horseback riding with his wife and fell, breaking two ribs under his right arm; worried the injury would remove him from the mission, he had a civilian doctor in nearby Rosamond tape his ribs; to seal the hatch the pilot had to slam down a heavy lever with the right arm, so he secretly asked his friend and fellow project pilot Jack Ridley, who sawed off the end of a broom handle for him to use as a lever; flown over the Rogers Dry Lake, Mojave Desert; the X-1 named Glamorous Glennis after his wife Glennis; the success was not announced to the public for nearly eight months (10 June 1948); on 14 October 1997, the 50th anniversary, he flew an F-15D past Mach 1 (born 13 February 1923)
Wikipedia: Bell X-1 — a rocket plane, in principle a 'bullet with wings', its shape closely resembling a Browning .50-calibre machine-gun bullet; drop-launched from the bomb bay of a B-29
Also on this day (candidates.md, in the app): 1066 the Battle of Hastings; 1926 the first Winnie-the-Pooh book is published
Archive film (public domain): US Air Force, 'Chuck Yeager Breaking The Sound Barrier 1947' (Air Photographic and Charting Service)

Photos (public domain / CC0): Yeager in the X-1 cockpit; Captain Charles E. Yeager; Yeager beside Glamorous Glennis; the X-1's nose art and hatch (Bell Aircraft, 1946); Yeager, Gus Lundquist and James Fitzgerald, 1947; the X-1 in the belly of a B-29; the X-1 in flight
Illustrative stock footage (Pexels, free licence; not of the event): a rider and horse at sunset
Photo (public domain, USAF): Yeager prepares to board an F-15D, 14 October 2012

post.facebook:
On this day in 1947, Captain Chuck Yeager became the first person to officially fly faster than sound.

Two nights before the flight, he went riding with his wife, fell off a horse and broke two ribs. Worried he would be taken off the mission, he had a civilian doctor in nearby Rosamond tape them up. But to seal the hatch of the Bell X-1, the pilot had to slam down a heavy lever with his right arm — so his friend and fellow pilot Jack Ridley sawed off the end of a broom handle for him to use as a lever.

A B-29 carried the X-1 — a rocket plane shaped like a .50-calibre bullet, named Glamorous Glennis after Yeager's wife — and dropped it over the Mojave Desert. At 45,000 feet, Yeager went supersonic. The success was kept from the public for nearly eight months.

Fifty years later, on 14 October 1997, he flew past Mach 1 again, in an F-15. He was 74.

Also on 14 October: the Battle of Hastings (1066), and the first Winnie-the-Pooh book (1926).

youtube.description:
14 October 1947: two nights before the flight, test pilot Chuck Yeager fell off a horse and broke two ribs. He hid it, had a civilian doctor tape him up, and closed the Bell X-1's hatch with a sawed-off broom handle his friend Jack Ridley made for him. Dropped from a B-29 over the Mojave Desert, he became the first man to fly faster than sound — and the world wasn't told for nearly eight months. Fifty years later to the day, at 74, he did it again.

Also on 14 October: the Battle of Hastings (1066) and the first Winnie-the-Pooh book (1926).
